Technologically, bus-rapid transit may be better suited than rail-rapid transit for a low density area. Since population density is low the busses provide local service in tributary areas near the freeway. A rail-rapid transit system cannot expect high patronage in low-density areas.

The Northwestern University study further states:
Most of the growth in auto travel in the Chicago Area is estimated to occur in outlying areas. By 1980, total vehicle miles of travel by auto is expected to almost double with 28% moving over the presently planned mileage of freeways.
New freeways and improvements to arterial street systems will be needed to accommodate the doubling of auto travel. Some of the additional radial freeways should contain provisions for rapid transit operations (via rail or bus-rapid transit) with facilities so designed that overloads on freeways will not impede rapid transit operations.<sup>2</sup>
